sumber: KSSM Form 1 English DSKP (CEFR-aligned). All passages and questions are written for the app.

nota.t: Tenses show when an action happens. Use the present simple for habits and facts, the present continuous for actions happening now, the past simple for finished actions and the future (will / going to) for plans and predictions.
Questions and negatives in the past use did + base verb: Did she go? She didn't go.

Nouns name people, places and things; they can be countable (an apple, two apples) or uncountable (water). Articles a and an go with singular countable nouns, the with specific ones. Pronouns such as he, them and its replace nouns.

t: a/an for one of many; the for a specific thing.
Countable: many, a few. Uncountable: much, a little.

nota.t: Comparatives compare two things (taller, more beautiful) and superlatives compare three or more (the tallest, the most beautiful). Modals such as can, must, should and may show ability, obligation, advice and possibility.

t: -er / -est for short adjectives; more / most for long ones.
Modals + base verb: can, could, must, should, might, will.

nota.t: Vocabulary grows by learning words in groups: synonyms (big, large), antonyms (hot, cold), collocations (make a decision), phrasal verbs (look after) and word families (happy, happiness, unhappy).

t: Idioms and phrasal verbs (look after, give up).

nota.t: The main idea is what a text is mostly about; it is often in the first or last sentence of a paragraph. Skim the title, headings and topic sentences to find it quickly.
Reading for details means scanning for specific facts such as names, numbers, dates and places. Read the question first, then look for key words in the text.
Inference means understanding what the writer suggests but does not say directly. Use clues in the text, such as a character's actions and words, together with your own knowledge.
Everyday speaking functions include greeting, introducing yourself, asking for and giving directions, and making polite requests. Use clear pronunciation, suitable expressions and good manners.
To give opinions use phrases like 'I think…' or 'In my opinion…', and support them with reasons. To make requests, use 'Could you…?' or 'Would you mind…?'. Listen to others and respond politely.
Different texts have different formats: an informal letter or email to a friend, a notice, an invitation, a short story and a review. Each has its own layout, opening, closing and style.
A good paragraph has a topic sentence, supporting sentences with details or examples, and a concluding sentence. Use linking words such as firstly, however and finally.
Poems use rhythm, rhyme and imagery to share feelings and ideas. Look for the theme, the poet's message and literary devices such as similes, metaphors and personification.
Short stories have characters, a setting, a plot (beginning, conflict, climax, resolution) and a theme. Think about how the characters change and what lesson the story teaches.

v.c: The plot of a short story

t: Skim for the main idea; scan for details (names, numbers).
Look for reason words: because, so, as.
Infer feelings and character from actions.
Capital letters, full stops, commas, question marks and speech marks.
Linking words: first, then, because, so, but, however.
